statement: Whether serotonin transporter binding returns to normal after people stop using ecstasy has not been established, because no study has scanned the same people during use and again after a long break. Three findings are read as recovery: in 12 men who had not used MDMA for at least a year (mean 2.7 years), binding did not differ from that of men who used other drugs or none (F=1.22, p=0.31), although only one cortical region was measured and there was no group of people currently using (Selvaraj et al., 2009); in 24 people scanned once, binding was higher in those whose last dose was longer ago in pallidostriatum (0.14 binding-potential units per doubling of days, 95% CI 0.05-0.23), amygdala and thalamus but not in neocortex, from which the authors extrapolate a return to the comparison group's average after about 212 days, with a lower limit of 91 days and an upper limit beyond a human lifespan (Erritzoe et al., 2011); and in 23 people, global binding with one of two tracers was higher with longer abstinence (r=0.418 and 0.494, one-tailed p=0.026 and p<0.010) (McCann et al., 2005). Against these, two studies found no relation between binding and time since last use: 49 people abstinent a median of 38 days (range 11-194) (Kish et al., 2010) and 13 people abstinent 2 to 8 weeks (Urban et al., 2012); and a SPECT study in which the women who had stopped for at least a year had higher binding than the women still using heavily (difference 0.137, 95% CI 0.046-0.227) and did not differ from the comparison group, while remaining non-significantly lower in the two posterior cortical regions, compared separately recruited groups rather than the same people (Reneman et al., 2001). All of these comparisons are between people, so they cannot separate recovery from a difference between those who stop and those who do not, and the regions said to recover are not the regions where the difference is largest. A review of this literature nonetheless summarizes it as recovery within 40 to 200 days (Vegting et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Nobody knows whether the serotonin marker goes back to normal after people stop using ecstasy. No one has been scanned both while using and again years later. Three studies compared different people and found more of the marker in those who had stopped longer ago. Two others found no link with time since the last dose. People who stop may also be different from people who keep going, and the deeper parts of the brain, where the marker looked more normal, are not where the difference is biggest.
population: Adults who formerly used ecstasy, or who are abstinent for weeks to years when scanned
exposure: Longer time since the last dose of ecstasy
comparator: People still using ecstasy, or shorter abstinence, or people who have not used it
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Not estimable within a person, since no one has been scanned twice. Between people: +0.14 binding-potential units per doubling of days since last use in pallidostriatum (95% CI 0.05-0.23), +0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21), +0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22), and +0.005 in neocortex (-0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67), with an extrapolated return to the comparison average at about 212 days (lower limit 91 days, upper limit beyond a lifespan) (Erritzoe et al., 2011); correlations of global binding with months abstinent r=0.418 and 0.494, one-tailed (McCann et al., 2005); no relation at all in two studies with abstinence windows of 11-194 days and 2-8 weeks (Kish et al., 2010; Urban et al., 2012); and no difference from controls in 12 men abstinent at least a year, with no estimate or interval printed (Selvaraj et al., 2009).

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 356, time since last use); Results, 'SERT binding', 2nd paragraph and Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 357)
evidence.extracted: 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions and had stopped for a mean of 2.74 years (range 390-1825 days) did not differ in [11C]DASB binding from 9 men who used other drugs and 19 who used none (group F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31; region-by-group F=0.36, p=0.81), with no regional estimates or intervals printed. The authors state the result can mean either that binding never differed or that it recovered, and prefer recovery; there was no group of people currently using MDMA, and cortical analysis was limited to the frontal cortex.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 564, the drug group); Results, 'SERT binding', 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 568); Figure 4 and its caption (p. 569)
evidence.extracted: Across 24 people scanned once, binding was higher the longer ago the last MDMA dose was taken: per doubling of days, +0.14 binding-potential units in pallidostriatum (95% CI 0.05-0.23, p=0.004), +0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21, p=0.008), +0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22, p=0.046), and no relation in neocortex (+0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67). Adjusted for lifetime tablets, pallidostriatum (p=0.02), amygdala (p=0.02) and midbrain (p=0.02) held and thalamus did not. From a log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would reach the comparison average after about 212 days, with a lower 95% limit of 91 days and an upper limit beyond a human lifespan.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 1744, abstinence); Results, last paragraph (p. 1745, correlations)
evidence.extracted: In 23 people abstinent a mean of 4.7 months (SD 8.7), global [11C]McN5652 binding was higher with longer abstinence (specific distribution volume r=0.418, p=0.026; distribution volume ratio r=0.494, p<0.010), on one-tailed tests; no such correlation is reported for [11C]DASB. The authors call these analyses exploratory and underpowered.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1785, days withdrawn); Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 5th paragraph (p. 1787); Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes…' (p. 1792)
evidence.extracted: In 49 people abstinent a median of 38 days (range 11-194), there was no significant correlation between withdrawal time and binding in any region; the authors say the question of recovery could not be addressed because typical withdrawal was only 1-2 months, and cite the study of people abstinent about 2.7 years as suggesting any reduction might be reversible in some people.

In 13 people abstinent 2 to 8 weeks (mean 5.7), no correlation between length of abstinence and transporter or 5-HT2A binding reached significance; the authors note their narrow range of abstinence, and argue that the null result in men abstinent for a year cannot show recovery because that study had no group of people currently using and because cortical measurement with this tracer is noisy.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1865, time since last tablet); Table 3 and Table 4 (p. 1866); Results, last paragraph and Discussion (p. 1867)
evidence.extracted: With SPECT, 16 people who had used at least 50 tablets and had stopped for at least a year (mean 29 months) were compared with separately recruited groups: among women, overall binding was higher than in those still using heavily (difference 0.137, 95% CI 0.046-0.227, p=0.004) and did not differ from the comparison group (0.031, -0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524), while remaining non-significantly lower in parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107). Nobody was scanned twice; the Discussion states that a prospective design would be needed to establish reversibility. (the Lancet prints decimal points as middle dots, so these values appear in the PDF as 0·168 and so on.)

The review summarizes the field as showing that transporter binding recovers after 40 to 200 days, the 40 days coming from a baboon study in which binding rose in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but stayed low in cortex, and the 200 days from the cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex. It then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurones, noting a study in which memory scores stayed low although binding had normalized, and concludes that the cause of any recovery is unknown.

risk_of_bias.note: Every estimate compares different people: those who have stopped may differ from those who continue in how much they used, in why they stopped and in everything else they take. Abstinence is self-reported except for the weeks before scanning, two of the analyses are one-tailed, and the study of people abstinent for a year prints no estimates or intervals.

inconsistency.note: Three studies report a relation with time since last use and two find none; the regions in which binding looks recovered (pallidostriatum, amygdala, thalamus) are not those in which the difference is largest, and the one study of long abstinence measured only one cortical region.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded again: the between-person design is already counted under risk of bias.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded again; the width of the one published extrapolation (91 days to beyond a lifespan) is stated in the claim.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (all comparisons are between people, with self-reported abstinence and one-tailed tests) and inconsistency (two studies find no relation with time since last use, and the regions that look recovered are not the ones most affected). The claim is worded as insufficient evidence, which is what the designs support: absence of a difference in people who stopped long ago is not evidence that binding recovered in them.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The two longitudinal studies the review cites (Buchert et al., 2006, and Thomasius et al., 2006, in which some people were scanned more than once) have not been read; they should be obtained before this claim is shown, since they are the only designs that could answer the question from within people.

changelog.change: Drafted (AI reader 45, MDMA batch 5a) from six primary imaging studies read in full plus the molecular-imaging review, to answer whether the transporter difference goes away after people stop.
